context_question: What are the primary goals and success criteria for SPRAT from the stakeholders’ perspective?
answer:
From our perspective, SPRAT should make it much easier for analysts to connect security and privacy requirements back to the policies and legal obligations they came from, without losing traceability. It also needs to support collaboration, so different people can work on the same analysis, compare their results, and spot gaps or inconsistencies quickly.
We’d consider it successful if teams can produce more complete and consistent analyses in less time, with clear evidence of how each requirement was derived. Another big sign of success would be that people with different roles can use it appropriately, with access controlled in a way that protects sensitive information but doesn’t slow down the work.

context_question: What boundary conditions, exceptions, or special cases should SPRAT handle for the analysis process—for example, incomplete or conflicting source policies, missing legal obligations, partial analyses, or cases where traceability cannot be established?
answer:
Yes, those situations do come up, and SPRAT should handle them explicitly instead of forcing analysts to pretend everything is complete. If a source policy is incomplete or a legal obligation is missing, the system should let the analyst flag that gap, record assumptions, and mark the item as unresolved so it’s visible in the analysis.
For conflicting policies or requirements, SPRAT should allow both versions to be captured and highlight the conflict so a reviewer can resolve it later. And if traceability can’t be established for something, that should be treated as a documented exception, not silently ignored, so partial analyses are still usable and clearly labeled as partial.

context_question: When analysts compare or update analyses over time, how should SPRAT manage analysis versions—for example, should it keep full histories of changes, allow branching or merging, identify who changed what and when, and let users compare earlier versions side by side?
answer:
We do need a full history of changes, because in practice people will want to see how an analysis evolved and who made each change. It should identify the user, the timestamp, and ideally the reason for the change if they provide one, since that helps with review and accountability.
Side-by-side comparison of earlier versions is important, especially for spotting differences in goals, requirements, or trace links. Branching and merging might be useful, but I’d treat that as a nice-to-have unless teams are working in parallel a lot; I’m not sure we need full version-control style workflows on day one.

context_question: When an analyst changes a goal, requirement, policy link, or other analysis item in SPRAT, what review and approval workflow should that change follow before it becomes visible or final—for example, should changes be immediately saved, require peer review, or need explicit approval from a project manager or administrator?
answer:
The change should be saved immediately so the analyst doesn’t lose work, but it shouldn’t always be considered final right away. For most edits, I’d expect a draft or pending state until a review happens, especially when the change affects traceability, policy interpretation, or legal compliance.
I think peer review should be the normal path, with project managers stepping in for anything higher risk or contentious, and administrators only handling access or system-level issues. The exact approval rule probably depends on the project’s configuration, because not every team will want the same level of control.

context_question: How should SPRAT manage the draft or pending state for changes after they are saved—for example, what actions are allowed while an item is still draft, what makes it transition to reviewed or final, and who can see or edit it at each stage?
answer:
While something is in draft or pending, the analyst who created it should be able to keep editing it and probably withdraw or revise it before review. Other analysts and project managers should at least be able to see that it exists, but I’d expect visibility to be limited if the item contains sensitive material or has not been approved yet.
It should move to reviewed or final only after the required reviewer signs off, and that approval should be recorded in the history. Once it’s final, edits should create a new revision rather than overwriting the approved one, so the approved version stays intact for audit and comparison.

context_question: For items that are still in draft or pending review, what exactly should other roles be able to see or do, and what rules should determine when the item’s content, metadata, or existence is visible versus hidden because it is sensitive or not yet approved?
answer:
Other roles should usually be able to see that a draft exists, who owns it, what it is roughly about, and its review status, but not necessarily the full content if it’s sensitive or still under discussion. I’d expect project managers and assigned reviewers to see more detail than general analysts, while guests should probably see nothing about drafts unless a project explicitly allows it.
As a rule, the item’s existence and basic metadata can be visible to people with the right project access, but the content itself should be hidden until it is approved or explicitly shared. If an item is marked sensitive, then even the metadata may need to be limited to only the author, reviewers, and admins.

context_question: Which external tools, repositories, or upstream systems should SPRAT be able to import analysis data from, and what kinds of imported content or structure must be preserved during that import?
answer:
We definitely expect SPRAT to import from common document sources and possibly spreadsheets or structured exports from other requirements tools, since a lot of analyses start outside the system. I’d also expect support for importing policy or compliance references from upstream repositories if the team already maintains those separately, but I’m not sure we’ve narrowed down the exact systems yet.
What matters most is preserving the structure of the analysis, not just the text, so goals, scenarios, requirements, policy links, and traceability need to come across intact. If there are classifications, tags, or version references in the source, those should be retained too where possible, though we may need to map them if the source format doesn’t match SPRAT exactly.

context_question: Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about your project needs so we can understand the requirements clearly and avoid missing anything important. Before we begin, are you aligned with this interview scope, or do you expect something different?
answer: Yes, I’m aligned with that scope. We’re focused on understanding what SPRAT needs to support collaborative requirements and privacy analysis, especially around capturing artifacts, tracing them to policies, and handling different user roles.

context_question: Thank you. To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?
answer: I’m one of the stakeholders responsible for privacy and security analysis in this project. I work with the analysts and project managers who would actually use SPRAT to document requirements, connect them to policies, and review the analyses together.

context_question: Understood. Could you please describe the current process or tools you use today for capturing requirements, policies, and traces between them?
answer: Right now, most of it is spread across documents, spreadsheets, and email threads, so it’s pretty manual. People capture requirements in one place, keep policy references somewhere else, and then try to maintain traceability by hand, which makes comparisons and reviews difficult.

context_question: What current processes do you want to change or improve, or what features are you hoping to get from SPRAT?
answer: We want to centralize the whole analysis workflow so people can capture goals, scenarios, policies, requirements, and compliance notes in one place. The big improvement is making traceability and comparison easier, especially when different analysts produce slightly different interpretations. We also want the classifications to be flexible enough to match the way our teams actually work.

context_question: So far, I understand these main needs: centralized capture of goals, scenarios, policies, requirements, and compliance notes; easier traceability between requirements and source policies; comparison of analyses from different people; and flexible classifications. Are there any other main features you would like SPRAT to have?
answer: Yes, role-based access is important too. Administrators, project managers, analysts, and guests should not all see or edit the same things, and we need a clear way to control that. It would also help if the tool supported collaboration without overwriting each other’s work.

context_question: Based on your description, do you think versioning or change-history tracking should also be included to help prevent people from overwriting each other’s work and to make collaboration safer?
answer: Yes, definitely. We would want to see who changed what and when, and ideally be able to go back if something was entered incorrectly or replaced by mistake. That would make the collaboration much safer and easier to review.

context_question: So the main features/functions are: centralized artifact capture, traceability to policies, comparison of different analyses, flexible classifications, role-based access control, collaboration without overwrites, and versioning/change history with rollback. Are there any other features you would like to see in this project?
answer: I think those are the main ones. Anything beyond that would be nice to have, but I’d need to check with the team before saying it’s required.

context_question: Which of these main features would you prioritize first for SPRAT?
answer: I’d put centralized capture and traceability first, because without those the rest doesn’t really have a solid foundation. Right after that, I’d prioritize role-based access and change history, since those are important for safe day-to-day use. Comparison of analyses and flexible classifications are also important, but I’d place them a little later if we had to sequence the work.

context_question: For centralized capture and traceability, could you describe the specific artifacts SPRAT needs to store and link, such as goals, scenarios, policies, requirements, and compliance notes?
answer: We’d need to store goals at a high level, then the scenarios or use cases that explain how those goals are realized. We also need the actual requirements, both security and privacy related, plus the policies or legal sources they come from, and any compliance notes or rationale that explain why a requirement exists. The key thing is that each of those artifacts should be linkable to each other, especially from a requirement back to the source policy or legal reference.

context_question: Could you describe how you want those artifacts to be linked and traced, especially from a requirement back to its source policy or legal reference?
answer: Ideally, the links should be explicit and navigable, so if I open a requirement I can immediately see which policy, regulation, or internal rule justified it. I’d also want the trace to work both ways, so from a policy or legal reference I can see all the requirements that came from it. If there are multiple sources, the system should show that clearly instead of forcing one single parent.

context_question: What should happen when a requirement has multiple source policies or legal references—should SPRAT let users choose one primary source, or treat all sources equally?
answer: I’d treat all sources as valid, but it would still be useful to let users mark one as primary for convenience or reporting. In practice, some requirements come from several overlapping policies, and we shouldn’t lose that detail just to force a single origin. So the system should keep the full set of sources and allow one to be highlighted if needed.

answer: Yes, this tool is meant to help analysts work together on web-system requirements and make sure those requirements line up with privacy and security policies from the start. answer: The main goal is to help analysts produce privacy- and security-aware requirements faster and with fewer mistakes. We also want strong traceability, so people can see why a requirement exists and which policy or legal obligation it came from. Another big goal is collaboration and comparison, because different analysts may produce different interpretations and we need the tool to make those differences visible and manageable.

context_question: You mentioned helping analysts work faster and with fewer mistakes, which sounds great. Could you share what measurable business outcomes or key performance indicators you’d like SPRAT to help achieve? answer: We’d like to reduce the time it takes to complete an analysis, but I don’t have an exact target number yet. A practical measure would be fewer missing traces between requirements and source policies, and fewer issues found later during review or compliance checking. I’d also expect better consistency between analysts, though I’d need to check with the team before naming any formal KPI targets.

context_question: Thanks for sharing those practical measures. To help me understand the environment SPRAT will operate in, could you describe any assumptions you have about the system context? answer: We expect it to fit into our existing requirements and project workflows, so analysts should be able to use it alongside whatever document or issue-tracking tools the team already relies on. I’m not sure yet whether we need direct integrations with specific external systems, but import and export will definitely matter so people can move information in and out without rekeying everything.
